what: EnerSys is the world’s largest maker of industrial batteries. It makes reserve power batteries and energy systems for telecom networks, data centres and utilities, motive power batteries and chargers for forklifts and warehouse vehicles, and specialty batteries for aerospace, defence and heavy trucks. Its fiscal year ends in March.
customers: Telecom and cable operators, data-centre and UPS makers, utilities, warehouse and logistics operators, forklift manufacturers, defence contractors and truck makers.
money: Batteries and power systems for telecom, data centres, broadband and utilities.
Lead-acid and lithium batteries and chargers for forklifts and material-handling equipment.
Batteries for aerospace, defence and transportation.
moat: Industrial batteries need to be reliable for decades, so customers buy from proven suppliers with global service networks. EnerSys has scale, a large installed base for replacement sales and certifications in defence and telecom that are hard to win. Its main weakness is that lead-acid technology is mature and the shift to lithium brings new competitors.
risks: Lead-acid demand faces a long-term shift to lithium, where Asian cell makers dominate.
Telecom spending has been weak, hurting Energy Systems volumes.
Part of recent profit comes from US 45X advanced manufacturing tax credits, which could change with policy.
Lead prices and commodity costs swing margins.
A planned US lithium cell factory was paused, slowing its lithium strategy.
opportunities: Data-centre power demand from AI is a large new market for its energy systems.
Free cash flow over the last twelve months was $650M, about 14% of the market value.
The shares trade at about 13 times trailing and 9 times forward earnings, and 8 times EV/EBITDA.
Buybacks cut the share count from 43M to 38M since fiscal 2022.
watch: Data-centre orders, telecom recovery, the size of 45X credits in earnings, lithium product progress and buybacks.
view: EnerSys is priced like a dying lead-acid business, and it is not quite that. Gross margin has risen from 22% to 29% since fiscal 2022 as the mix moved to higher-value systems, and cash generation has been strong: operating cash flow of $701M and free cash flow of $650M over the last twelve months against a $4.6B market value. Few industrial companies trade at a 14% free cash flow yield.

Two adjustments are needed. First, US 45X production credits have flattered profits since 2023; they are real cash today but depend on tax policy, so I would not value them at the same multiple as operating earnings. Second, free cash flow is lumpy, it was only $139M in fiscal 2025, so the last twelve months are near the top of the range. Even normalising both, the stock trades on about 9 times forward earnings.

The investment turns on whether data-centre and defence demand can offset the slow decline of traditional telecom and forklift lead-acid sales. AI data centres need backup power and the defence business is growing, which gives EnerSys a credible path. The analyst target near $232 looks optimistic, but at this price you are paid to wait. I think the stock is undervalued for a company with this cash generation.
bull: Data-centre and defence growth outweighs lead-acid decline and strong cash flow funds steady buybacks.
bear: Lithium competition erodes the core business and 45X credits fade, removing a large part of current profit.
